title: Introduction to C++
goal: Write, compile and run your first C++ program, and understand what the compiler and linker each do.

topics.title: Your first C++ program
topics.body: Every C++ program starts at `main`. `std::cout` writes text to the terminal; `<<` sends the value into the stream and `\n` ends the line.

topics.title: Compile, link, run
topics.body: The compiler turns source into an object file, the linker joins it with the standard library, and the loader runs the executable. `g++ main.cpp -o app` does all three.

topics.title: The compiler is your first reader
topics.body: C++ is statically typed: the compiler checks types before anything runs. An `int` occupies four bytes on this compiler, which `sizeof` reports.

debug.title: iostream never included
debug.error: error: ‘cout’ is not a member of ‘std’

tasks.title: Print a two-line banner
tasks.statement: Print "BroCode C++" on the first line and "26 modules" on the second, then return 0.

interviewBank.q: What happens between the source file and a running program?
interviewBank.answer: Preprocessing expands includes and macros, compilation translates each translation unit to an object file, the linker resolves symbols against libraries, and the loader maps the executable into memory before `main` runs. A missing function definition fails at link time, not compile time.

The return value is the process exit status: 0 means success and a non-zero value reports failure to the shell and to whatever script launched the program. `return 0;` at the end of main is implicit, but writing it makes the intent explicit.

defenseBank.q: A new learner asks why their code does not run after saving the file. What do you check first?
defenseBank.answer: Saving is not compiling. I check whether a compiler was actually invoked and whether the binary they ran is the one just built.
steps: Confirm the compile command and its exit status.
Confirm the path of the binary that was executed.
Read the first compiler error, not the last.

defenseBank.q: Why teach `std::cout` instead of `using namespace std;`?
defenseBank.answer: The `std::` prefix keeps every name visible at its use site and avoids the collisions that a global using-directive invites. For a beginner the extra five characters are cheaper than a name clash they cannot diagnose.

mini.title: Hello, environment
mini.brief: Write a program that prints your name, the C++ standard you compiled with (`__cplusplus`) and the size of an int.
steps: Include iostream and start main.
Print the three values on separate lines.
Return 0 and compile with g++ -std=c++17.

lab.title: Build-and-run checklist
lab.brief: Produce a one-screen checklist that takes a source file to a running program, and prove each step with real output.
milestones: Compile a file and show the compiler's exit status.
Run the binary and show its stdout.
Introduce a deliberate error and show the compiler's first message.

title: Program Structure and Input/Output
goal: Read the parts of a C++ program and take typed input from the user without leaving the stream broken.

topics.title: Reading input with cin
topics.body: `std::cin >> x` skips whitespace and reads one value into `x`. Reading into a string stops at the first space, which is why full names need `getline`.

topics.title: getline reads the whole line
topics.body: `std::getline(std::cin, line)` keeps spaces. Mixing `>>` and `getline` leaves a newline in the buffer, so consume it first.

topics.title: Formatting output
topics.body: `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision` come from `<iomanip>` and control decimals; the setting persists until you change it.

debug.title: A number assigned to a string
debug.error: error: conversion from ‘int’ to non-scalar type ‘std::string’ {aka ‘std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>’} requested

debug.title: setprecision without iomanip
debug.error: error: ‘setprecision’ is not a member of ‘std’

tasks.title: Add two numbers
tasks.statement: Start from 12 and 8, print their sum.

interviewBank.q: Why does `cin >> name` lose the second word of a full name?
interviewBank.answer: Formatted extraction treats whitespace as a delimiter: it reads until the next space and leaves the rest in the buffer. `getline` reads to the newline instead, which is the correct tool for a line of text.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `\n` and `std::endl`?
interviewBank.answer: Both write a newline, but `std::endl` also flushes the stream. Flushing every line is unnecessary in most code and costs performance in loops, so `\n` is the default choice.

defenseBank.q: A menu program loops forever after a bad input. Explain the cause.
defenseBank.answer: When extraction fails, `cin` sets its failbit and leaves the bad characters in the buffer, so the next read fails immediately. The fix is to detect failure, clear the state and ignore the rest of the line.
steps: Check `if (!std::cin)` after every read.
Call `std::cin.clear()` and `std::cin.ignore(...)`.
Re-prompt instead of proceeding with an unsent value.

defenseBank.q: Why is input validation part of the lesson, not an advanced extra?
defenseBank.answer: A program that trusts its input is a program that corrupts its own state on the first typo. Validation is cheaper to teach at the point of input than to debug later as a mysterious loop.

steps: Read the line with getline, then the numbers.

title: Variables, Data Types and Constants
goal: Choose a type deliberately, know its range and size, and keep values that must not change constant.

topics.title: The numeric types
topics.body: `int` is the default whole number; `double` is the default decimal. `long long` exists because `int` is not guaranteed to hold a large id.

topics.title: char, bool and their limits
topics.body: `char` stores one character code, `bool` stores true or false, and `sizeof` reports the storage each type takes.

topics.title: const and auto
topics.body: `const` makes a name read-only and lets the compiler reject an accidental write. `auto` asks the compiler to deduce the type from the initializer, which is a tool for long types, not for hiding them.

debug.title: Writing to a const
A string literal assigned to a char
debug.error: error: invalid conversion from ‘const char*’ to ‘char’ [-fpermissive]

tasks.title: Average without integer division
tasks.statement: Average the marks 70, 80 and 90 and print it with two decimals.

interviewBank.q: Why is `double` the default for decimals instead of `float`?
interviewBank.answer: `double` has roughly twice the precision and is the type of unsuffixed floating literals, so it avoids the silent rounding that `float` introduces in ordinary calculations. `float` is for storage-sensitive cases, not the default.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between initialization and assignment?
interviewBank.answer: Initialization gives a variable its first value as it is created; assignment replaces a value that already exists. A `const` can be initialized but never assigned, which is why the distinction matters to the compiler.

defenseBank.q: Why is an uninitialized local variable dangerous even when the program seems to run?
defenseBank.answer: Its value is indeterminate, so reading it is undefined behaviour: the output can change between builds, compilers and optimisation levels. A test that passes today proves nothing about it.
steps: Name the undefined behaviour, not just the wrong number.
Show the fix: initialize at declaration.
Explain why the bug is not reproducible.

defenseBank.answer: When it hides a conversion or an ownership decision the reader needs to see. `auto x = 1.5;` is fine; `auto p = makeWidget();` is only fine if the widget type is obvious from the name.

title: Operators and Type Conversion
goal: Use arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators without falling into integer division or implicit-conversion traps.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus
topics.body: Two ints divide as integers and discard the remainder. Convert one side to `double` when you need the fractional part; `%` gives the remainder.

topics.title: Comparison and logic
topics.body: Comparisons produce bools, `&&` and `||` combine them with short-circuit evaluation, and `!` negates. A chained comparison like `1 < x < 3` does not mean what it looks like.

topics.title: Bitwise operators
topics.body: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>` work on the bits of an integer. They are used for flags and masks, and they are not the same as the logical operators.

debug.title: Modulus on a double
debug.error: error: invalid operands of types ‘double’ and ‘int’ to binary ‘operator%’

debug.title: A chained comparison
debug.error: Wrong output: 1 — `1 < x < 3` compares the bool `1 < x` with 3, so it is always true.

tasks.title: Grade from marks
tasks.statement: Starting from 72 marks, print A for 90+, B for 70+, C for 50+, otherwise fail.

interviewBank.answer: Both operands are ints, so the division is integer division and the fractional part is discarded. Making one operand a double, for example `7 / 2.0`, selects floating-point division.

interviewBank.q: When is `static_cast` preferable to a C-style cast?
interviewBank.answer: `static_cast` states which conversion is intended and is checked at compile time for incompatible types, so a reviewer can see it. A C-style cast can silently become a reinterpret_cast, which is much harder to justify.

defenseBank.q: A learner writes `int avg = total / count;` and the average is wrong. What do you ask?
defenseBank.answer: I ask for the types of total and count before touching the formula: if both are integers, the division already lost the fraction before the assignment.
steps: Check the operand types, not the variable being assigned.
Check for a divide-by-zero path.
Convert one operand and re-test with a case that has a remainder.

defenseBank.q: Why are implicit conversions a common source of bugs?
defenseBank.answer: They are invisible at the call site, so a `double` narrowing to `int` or a negative `int` converting to `unsigned` reads like a normal assignment. Braces and explicit casts make the conversion visible.

title: Conditional Statements
goal: Make decisions with if, else-if, switch and the ternary operator, including range checks and menu selection.

topics.title: if and else-if
topics.body: Only the first true branch runs. Order the ranges from most specific to least, because a later `else if` is only reached when the earlier ones were false.

topics.title: switch needs integral cases
topics.body: `switch` compares one integral value against constant cases. `break` leaves the switch; forgetting it falls through into the next case.

topics.title: The ternary operator
topics.body: `condition ? a : b` picks one of two values and is an expression, so it can initialize a variable. Keep it for short choices; a nested ternary is harder to read than an if.

debug.title: A string used as a case label
debug.error: error: switch quantity not an integer

debug.title: An else-if that can never run
debug.error: Wrong output: positive — the broad first branch swallows every value the specific branch was meant to catch.

tasks.title: Factorial with a loop

interviewBank.q: When should you prefer switch over if-else?
interviewBank.answer: When one integral value is compared against several constant alternatives and each branch is independent: the switch states the intent and the compiler can warn about a missing default. Ranges and non-integral types need if-else.
An `else` binds to the nearest unmatched `if`, which may not be the one the indentation suggests. Braces around every branch make the binding explicit.

defenseBank.q: Explain a menu-driven program to a beginner without showing code.
defenseBank.answer: It is a loop that shows numbered choices, reads the number, runs the matching branch and repeats until the user chooses exit. The loop is the part that keeps the menu alive; switch is only the dispatcher.
steps: Describe the loop and its exit condition.
Describe how a number selects a branch.
Describe what happens for an unknown number.

defenseBank.q: Why validate a range instead of trusting the branch order?
defenseBank.answer: Branch order encodes assumptions about the data. If a negative mark arrives, an ordered ladder may fall into a plausible-looking bucket, so an explicit range check is what makes the failure visible.

title: Loops and Iteration
goal: Repeat work with for, while and range-for, and know when break, continue and a sentinel make a loop clearer.

topics.title: The for loop
topics.body: A `for` loop names its counter, its bound and its step in one line, which makes the number of iterations readable at a glance.

topics.title: while and a sentinel
topics.body: `while` repeats while a condition holds. A sentinel value, such as -1, ends a read loop without needing to know the count in advance.

topics.title: Range-based for
topics.body: `for (int v : values)` visits each element without an index. Use `const auto&` when the elements are expensive to copy.

debug.title: A break outside any loop
debug.error: error: break statement not within loop or switch

debug.title: An off-by-one sum
debug.error: Wrong output: 10 — the loop stops before 5, so the last term is missing.

tasks.title: Greatest common divisor
tasks.statement: Print the GCD of 12 and 18 using a function.

interviewBank.q: When is a do-while the right loop?
interviewBank.answer: When the body must run at least once, such as showing a menu or reading a value before validating it. The condition is checked after the body, so the first pass is unconditional.

interviewBank.q: Why is `continue` sometimes a readability problem?
interviewBank.answer: It skips the rest of the body, so a reader has to hold every earlier continue in mind to know what actually executes. A guard clause or an if-else is often clearer.

defenseBank.q: A loop never ends. What is your debugging order?
defenseBank.answer: I check whether the condition can ever become false, then whether the counter is modified on every path, including the continue paths.
steps: Print the loop variables on the first few iterations.
Look for a continue that skips the update.
Check for a condition that compares the wrong variable.

defenseBank.q: Why is an off-by-one error so common at boundaries?
defenseBank.answer: Because the two conventions `<` and `<=` differ in exactly one case, and the difference only appears at the last iteration. Naming the bound as a count rather than an index removes the ambiguity.

title: Functions and Recursion
goal: Break a program into functions with clear parameters and return values, and use recursion with a real base case.

topics.title: Declare, define, call
topics.body: A declaration tells the compiler a function's signature; the definition supplies the body. The call site only needs the declaration, which is why headers work.

topics.title: Pass by reference
topics.body: A reference parameter aliases the caller's object, so the function can change it without pointers. `const&` avoids the copy but forbids the change.

topics.title: Recursion needs a base case
topics.body: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and stops at a base case. Without the base case the call stack grows until it overflows.

debug.title: A function used before it is declared
debug.error: error: ‘square’ was not declared in this scope

debug.title: A reference parameter changed by value
debug.error: Wrong output: 80 — the parameter is a copy, so the caller's marks never changed.

tasks.title: Greatest common divisor
tasks.statement: Print the GCD of 12 and 18 using a function.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
interviewBank.answer: A parameter is the variable in the function's signature; an argument is the value the caller supplies for it. The distinction matters when explaining overloading and default arguments.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `const std::string&` over `std::string` for a read-only parameter?
interviewBank.answer: The reference avoids copying the string, and `const` promises the function will not modify the caller's object. For small types such as int the copy is cheaper than the indirection.

defenseBank.q: A recursive function crashes with a stack overflow. Explain the failure precisely.
defenseBank.answer: Every call keeps a stack frame alive until it returns, so a missing or unreachable base case turns recursion into unbounded stack growth. The program aborts when the stack limit is reached.
steps: Show the base case and why it is not reached.
Trace the argument on the first three calls.
Fix the base case or convert to iteration.

defenseBank.q: When is iteration a better choice than recursion?
defenseBank.answer: When the recursive depth is linear and the problem needs no backtracking: a loop uses constant stack and is easier to reason about. Recursion earns its cost on trees, divide-and-conquer and backtracking.
